blocks.text: Most people who search this want one thing: a PNG on disk, with the size and settings they expect. Photoshop has two routes to that file, and they behave differently. Quick Export is one menu command that saves with defaults you set in advance. Export As opens a dialog where you choose the format and settings for each file. The steps below cover both routes, the places people get stuck, and what to try when Photoshop refuses to export.
Quick Export or Export As: which route to use

Use Quick Export when you export the same kind of file again and again. A web banner you rebuild every week is a good example. You set the format once, and the command handles the rest. You do not get a dialog each time, and that speed is the point.

Use Export As when each file needs its own choices. A single hero image for a landing page is one example. You open the dialog, pick PNG, read the settings, and export. It takes longer. You also see every setting before the file is written.

blocks.text: Set PNG export defaults in Export Preferences

Quick Export is only as good as its defaults. HowToGeek says the defaults for format, quality, save location, metadata and color space live at File > Export > Export Preferences. Set them once, before you rely on Quick Export for real work. Otherwise you may save PNGs in a folder you never check, with metadata you did not mean to keep.

Here is a worked example. Say you prepare images for a client website. Set the format to PNG, point the save location at the client's folder, and choose the metadata setting the client needs. Every Quick Export then lands in the right place. For a print file on another day, use Export As for that one job, so the website defaults stay put.
Review the defaults at the start of each project. A forgotten default is an easy way to get a file into the wrong place, and it is the first thing to check when a Quick Export looks off.
Where the Export Preferences menu lives on Mac

The sources disagree on the menu path. PSDVault says Edit > Preferences > Export. A search snippet quoting Adobe says Photoshop > Preferences > Export on macOS. Look in both menus. Whichever one holds Preferences should open a pane called Export.
Write down the path your copy uses. Menu labels can change between releases, and a note saves you a search next time.
Keyboard shortcut for Quick Export as PNG

No default Mac shortcut is confirmed here for Quick Export or Export As. Do not trust a shortcut from a cheat sheet until you see it in Adobe's own shortcut table or in your copy of the app. You can assign your own at Edit > Keyboard Shortcuts. Under File, find the item Quick Export as. HowToGeek uses ⌘⌃⇧S as its example.

Test any combination in a scratch file before you rely on it. If a key does nothing, another app or a macOS setting may already use it. Pick a combination you can remember, because a shortcut you forget saves no time.
A shortcut only saves clicks. It does not fix the defaults. A shortcut that exports to the wrong folder just does the wrong thing faster.
Using the Export As dialog for each file
Open the dialog with File > Export > Export As. Use the format list to choose PNG. Read the settings before you click Export. A quick check here saves a second export later.
Check the file name and the folder every time. Fields can look right because they were right last time, and that is how files land in the wrong place.
If you export the same image at a second size, give it a new file name. Overwriting the first version is an easy way to lose a file you still need.
Why PNG export fails in Photoshop

Most export failures come down to a short list. The app may be out of date, the scratch disk may be full, the GPU settings may be off, or a plug-in may get in the way. PSDVault lists fixes along these lines and says exports can fail silently when scratch space runs low.

The 20 GB number matters. PSDVault says you need at least 20 GB of free space on the scratch disk to avoid silent export failures. Check the drive Photoshop uses for scratch files, not only the drive that holds your documents. A nearly full drive can break a save that worked yesterday.

Next, look at GPU memory. PSDVault suggests setting GPU memory use to 70 to 80 percent. Open Preferences, then Performance, and check the GPU section. Change one setting at a time, then run the export again so you know which change helped.

Work through the fixes from cheapest to slowest. Quit Photoshop with ⌘Q and open it again. Then check for updates at Help > Updates. If the export still fails, test it in a new document. If the new document exports, the problem sits in the old file or its plug-ins, not in the app.

Disable plug-ins one at a time if the problem stays. If macOS blocks the save, the permission may be the cause, and the [full disk access guide](/how-to/grant-full-disk-access-in-photoshop) covers that. If nothing works, [reset preferences](/how-to/reset-preferences-in-photoshop), but write down any custom settings first.
Photoshop on Mac vs the web version

Adobe lists Photoshop on desktop, web and mobile. This page covers the desktop app on a Mac. Adobe's product page says the web version needs a plan or free trial before you can upload and edit your own photos. Guided tutorials work without an account.
Adobe's page does not say which features differ between the versions. Do not assume the web menus match these steps. Open the web app and check its File menu before you follow the steps here.
Check your Photoshop version before you follow the menus

Menu labels change between releases. CG Channel reports that Adobe released Photoshop 27.10 on Monday, August 31, 2026. The same report says Photoshop 27.10 needs macOS 14.0 or later. It does not mention changes to Export As or Quick Export.

If you are not sure which build you have, read [how to check your Photoshop version on Mac](/how-to/check-your-photoshop-version-in-photoshop). If you are behind, [update Photoshop on Mac](/how-to/update-photoshop-in-photoshop) before you troubleshoot. Newer releases may have come out since this page was written, so your menu may look slightly different.
Common PNG export mistakes in Photoshop

items: Exporting the wrong document. Check the title bar before you export so the right file is active.
Trusting an old default. Open Export Preferences at the start of each project.
Assuming a shortcut exists. None is confirmed here, so assign your own first.
Overwriting the first version. Give each size or setting its own file name.
Ignoring the scratch disk. Free space matters even when your documents have plenty of room.
Changing five settings at once. Change one, export, and check the result before the next change.

blocks.text: What Photoshop costs if you do not have it yet

Adobe's product page lists Photoshop standalone at US$22.99 a month on the annual plan billed monthly, or US$263.88 a year prepaid. It lists a Photography plan at US$19.99 a month. These are US prices as shown on that page, and they can change, so check the page before you buy.
Check your Adobe account first. You may already have Photoshop in a plan you pay for. Buying a second plan just to export one PNG is rarely worth it.
Where to go next after your PNG is exported

PNG export is often the last step in a bigger job. If the image is the wrong size, [resize an image in Photoshop on Mac](/how-to/resize-an-image-in-photoshop) first. If you need a cutout with transparency, read [how to remove a background in Photoshop on Mac](/how-to/remove-a-background-in-photoshop).

Daily users can look at [Photoshop for designers on Mac](/for/designers/photoshop), which covers workflow and shortcuts. For selections before a cutout, see [how to make a selection in Photoshop on Mac](/how-to/make-a-selection-in-photoshop).
Test one file before you run a batch. Open the PNG, check its size and edges, and only then repeat the export for the rest of the files.

faq.question: Is Quick Export the same as Export As in Photoshop?
faq.answer: No. Quick Export runs with the defaults you set in Export Preferences and does not show a dialog. Export As opens a dialog so you can choose the format and settings for each file.

faq.question: Where is Quick Export in Photoshop on Mac?
faq.answer: Click File, point to Export, then choose Quick Export as PNG. Photoshop asks for a save location. Pick a folder and click Save.

faq.question: Does Photoshop have a default shortcut for PNG export?
faq.answer: No default Mac shortcut is confirmed on this page. Adobe's own shortcut table was not available to check when it was written. You can assign your own at Edit > Keyboard Shortcuts, under File, in the item Quick Export as.

faq.question: Why does my PNG export fail without an error message?
faq.answer: PSDVault says low scratch disk space can cause silent failures and recommends at least 20 GB free. Check the scratch disk, quit and reopen Photoshop, then test the export in a new document.

faq.question: Which version of Photoshop do I need for these steps?
faq.answer: CG Channel reports that Photoshop 27.10, released August 31, 2026, needs macOS 14.0 or later. Adobe's product page does not list version numbers, so compare your menus with the version guide linked on this page.

faq.question: Can I export a PNG in the web version of Photoshop?
faq.answer: Adobe says Photoshop runs on desktop, web and mobile. Its product page does not list export differences between them, so check the File menu in the version you use before you follow these steps.

faq.question: What if my menu shows Export As (Legacy)?
faq.answer: Some guides place the legacy dialog in the File menu. Others describe a toggle called Use legacy Export As in Preferences > Export. Use it only when the newer dialog fails, and confirm the label on your copy.

faq.question: How much does Photoshop cost on its own?
faq.answer: Adobe's product page lists Photoshop standalone at US$22.99 a month on the annual plan billed monthly, or US$263.88 a year prepaid. Prices can change, so check Adobe's page before you buy.

steps.name: Open the document you want to export
steps.text: Open the Photoshop file in the app. Check the title bar to confirm you have the right document. Turn off any layer you do not want in the PNG, using the eye icons in the Layers panel.
steps.tip: Look at the image on screen first. It should match what you expect in the PNG.

steps.name: Open the File menu and the Export submenu
steps.text: Click File in the menu bar at the top of the screen. Point at Export to open its submenu. Quick Export and Export As both live here.
steps.tip: If the labels look different on your copy, the menu may have changed in a newer release.

steps.name: Run Quick Export as PNG
steps.text: Click Quick Export as PNG. Photoshop asks where to save the file. Choose a folder, then click Save.
steps.tip: Quick Export uses the defaults in Export Preferences, so check those first.

steps.name: Choose Export As for more control
steps.text: Pick Export As when this file needs its own settings. The dialog opens. Choose PNG in the format list before you change anything else.
steps.tip: Skip this route if Quick Export already gives you the file you need.

steps.name: Find the Export pane in Preferences
steps.text: Open the Preferences window. Some guides list it under Edit, and others list it under Photoshop on macOS. Select the Export pane.
steps.tip: Note the path your copy uses, because menu labels can change.

steps.name: Set your export defaults
steps.text: Open Export Preferences. Set the format, quality, save location, metadata and color space you want as defaults. Close the window when the values match your plan.
steps.tip: Re-check the save location before each new project.

steps.name: Assign a shortcut to Quick Export
steps.text: Open Edit > Keyboard Shortcuts. Under File, find Quick Export as. Click the shortcut field for that item and press the keys you want. Then close the window.
steps.tip: HowToGeek uses ⌘⌃⇧S as an example. Test the combination in a scratch file first.

steps.name: Check the PNG outside Photoshop
steps.text: Open the exported file in Preview or drag it into a browser. Check the size, the edges, and any transparent areas. Compare them with what you saw on screen in Photoshop.
steps.tip: Checking in a second app shows you what the next person will see.

shortcuts.action: Quit Photoshop before you retry an export
Example from HowToGeek for a Quick Export shortcut, not an Adobe default

troubleshooting.problem: Quick Export exports to the wrong folder
troubleshooting.fix: Open File > Export > Export Preferences and check the format and save location. Run Quick Export again and check the folder before you move on.
Free at least 20 GB on the scratch disk, as PSDVault advises. Then quit Photoshop with ⌘Q, open it again, and try the export.

troubleshooting.problem: The Export As dialog misbehaves or shows an unknown error
troubleshooting.fix: Try the legacy dialog from Preferences > Export with Use legacy Export As, or from File > Export > Export As (Legacy) if your copy shows it. Confirm the path first.

troubleshooting.problem: Export still fails after a restart
troubleshooting.fix: Check for updates at Help > Updates, then test in a new document. If the new document exports, disable plug-ins one at a time to find the one that blocks the save.

troubleshooting.problem: Photoshop cannot save to the folder
troubleshooting.fix: Check the folder permissions and the macOS privacy settings. If macOS blocks the save, follow the full disk access guide linked in this page.

troubleshooting.problem: Export is slow or the GPU seems to cause trouble
troubleshooting.fix: Open Preferences > Performance, check the GPU settings, and set GPU memory use to 70 to 80 percent as PSDVault suggests. Test after each change.
